Preface by the Dharma-teacher Śramaṇa Changjin:
In the past, the Great Master, the World-Honored One, emitted a great radiance that illuminated the immeasurable,
boundless, and unspeakable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions— hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas, inconceivable and beyond calculation.
In immeasurable, unspeakable, and infinite asaṃkhyeya worlds, there is the emanation-body of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden arm, stroked the crown of the heads of the emanation-bodies of Kṣitigarbha in all those worlds, and said:

"You should remember: while I was in the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, I earnestly entrusted you with the task of causing all sentient beings from the Sahā world to attain liberation and forever leave behind all suffering.

When the Buddha granted me this prediction, the various transformation bodies of Kṣitigarbha from all worlds gathered at the Buddha’s location, merged into a single form, and with tears of sorrowful longing, spoke, saying: 'Since I have [come] from...'"
Since time immemorial, having been guided by the Buddhas, I have attained inconceivable spiritual powers and possess great wisdom.

My emanated bodies fill hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. In each world, I manifest hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodies;
and with each individual body, I deliver hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of people, causing them to take refuge in and revere the Triple Gem.

"May they forever leave behind birth and death and attain the bliss of nirvana. Whatever wholesome deeds they perform within the Buddha-dharma—be it a single hair, a single drop, a single grain of sand, a single speck of dust, or even the slightest fraction—I shall gradually deliver them and cause them to obtain great benefit.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will not worry about sentient beings with evil karma in future lives. Having thus addressed the Buddha three times, the Buddha immediately...
He gave his seal of approval and praised him, saying: "Excellent, Great Being! From now on, I shall have no further anxieties, nor shall sentient beings have any cause for concern.

Between the time that the Sage of Benevolence (Śākyamuni) has finished his work of transformation and before the World-Honored One of Compassion (Maitreya) awaits the proper opportunity, I entrust all those who are without refuge or protection—whether they be good or not so good, whether they be householders or those who have left the home life—to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva."
Indeed, it is precisely because that Great Being has manifested his response within this land that these sentient beings are likewise bound by causal conditions to that Sage.

Thus, those who fashion statues or paint images have their transformative influence filling their ears and eyes; those who invoke his name, pay homage, and make offerings have the efficacy of his miracles circulating on their lips.
Some record such superior benefits in ancient chronicles, while others note the descent of his spirit upon divination slips.
This brief record has barely reached one or two instances; it has not yet attained four or five. How much less could it encompass the full extent of his transmissions, insights, and experiences?
As for all his meritorious deeds, even these cannot be fully exhausted; therefore, they should be offered as an object of veneration.

Although this current collection of his final instructions constitutes a record, it is but a general outline and commentary—how could it ever exhaustively portray the man? Nevertheless, I have cited three or five examples to serve as a basis for faith and reliance.
In the year Jichou (609) of the Duan-gong era of the Great Song, the *Dharma-transmitting śramaṇa* Changjin compiled this record with his own hand.
First: An Account of the Radiant Earth Store Bodhisattva on the Wall of the Eastern Corridor at Shanji Monastery in the Liang Dynasty.
On the wall of the eastern corridor of Shanji Monastery in Deyang County, Hanzhou, during the Liang dynasty, there was Zhang Sengyou (Zhang Sengyou being a master painter).

On this [tablet] inscribed with the character "Zhi" (之), he painted one image each of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva and Avalokiteśvara. Their forms resembled those of monks, sitting with robes neatly folded and draped.

When people of the time gazed upon and prostrated before them, extraordinary radiance shone forth. In the first year of the Linde era, the monks of the temple, viewing them with reverence, marveled at how they differed from ordinary images.
Consequently, they took a piece of rice-cake paper to trace the forms from the wall and distributed them for offerings; they emitted light no differently than the originals. At that time—
There were many who successively copied [the image]. In the third year of the Linde era, Wang Ji was appointed as the Prefect of Zizhou.
He constantly made offerings with sincere devotion using copies [of the image]. While traveling on ten ships, they suddenly encountered a sudden gale; nine of the ships were submerged and drowned.
Amidst these surging waves, only Wang Ji’s ship experienced no fear whatsoever. One can thus know that the Bodhisattva’s [compassion] is vast and great.
Such is the majestic power of compassion. In the third year of the Chuigong era, Empress Wu heard of this and issued an imperial decree for an artist to copy it;
the image emitted light as before, and it was enshrined for veneration within the Daoist altar.

In the first year of the Dali era, a Great Virtue (Dade) of Baoshou Monastery beheld these extraordinary manifestations of light within the altar and submitted a memorial to inform the Emperor. The Emperor then paid homage with a devout heart.
Homage! One praises that light. When the Bodhisattva manifests this light, the kingdom is always peaceful and secure.

Furthermore, there was the wife of a merchant who had been pregnant for twenty-eight months without giving birth; she suddenly beheld the radiance and immediately sketched it. With single-minded devotion, she made a vow to the Bodhisattva.
That very night, she gave birth to a son whose physical marks were dignified and sublime, bringing joy to all who saw him throughout the world.
He is titled the Bodhisattva Emitting Light.
Second, the Record of the Painting of Kṣitigarbha Emitting Light at Faju Monastery in the Tang Dynasty.

At Faju Monastery under the capital of Yizhou during the Tang, an image of Kṣitigarbha was painted. Initially, he sat upon a corded chair with his feet hanging down, reaching a height of eight [units].
It measures sixteen *cun* and six *fen*. The original image was painted by Zhang Sengyou. In the seventh month of the second year of the Linde era, a monk of this temple obtained a copy;
it emitted light that appeared and disappeared intermittently, like a ring of refined gold, exactly like the light of the original.

All subsequent copies produced through successive transcriptions likewise emitted light. In the eighth month of that year, an imperial decree ordered one copy to be presented to the palace for veneration.
Yǎng. He presented these to secular painters within the capital for their veneration, and all of them emitted light.
One may truly know that the power of the Buddha is unfathomable. Each household produced a copy; those who obtained such a response are too numerous to be cited here.
The Third Record of the Earth Store Image for Saving from Suffering in the House of the Li Family of Hu County, Tang Dynasty.
In Hu County, Yongzhou of the Tang Dynasty, there was a woman named Lady Li who had long possessed faith in the Dharma and observed the precepts of the fast.

She possessed a wooden image of Earth Store (Kṣitigarbha) one foot and six inches in height, complete with its radiant halo and broad base; it manifested many miraculous signs. Lady Li had a maidservant.
He was over fifty years old and held heterodox views, having no faith in the True Dharma. While Li was away on a journey, she moved the statue and cast it into the wilderness behind her home.
When he returned and searched for it weeping, the statue was found in the field emitting light; he joyfully welcomed it back, unaware of what the maidservant had done.
The next day, the maidservant suddenly fell into a state of unconsciousness, and after being abandoned by the edge of the wilderness, she revived one day later.
Weeping and prostrating herself in repentance, she recounted her experiences on the path to the underworld, saying: "When I died, I suddenly saw two officials riding horses;
they presented me with official warrants and ordered me to read them. The messengers said, 'Slave girl! You have defiled and insulted sacred images and abandoned them in the wilderness.'"
"Since you have committed such a great crime, it is necessary to summon you before the royal court," they said. Having read the official decree, she was bound and led away.
Upon arriving before the royal court, she saw within the hall that her body was fettered with shackles, manacles, and neck-irons in measureless and boundless numbers—a state beyond description.
The King, filled with wrath, said: "You foolish slave! You have defiled the sacred countenance and cast it away into the wilderness; you must now suffer the retribution for this!"
[The King] arrived. He summoned her spirit, who cast herself down and abandoned her physical form. Furthermore, this woman lived at home with heterodox views and did not believe in the True Dharma;
she was destined for the Great Hell. At that time, a śramaṇa suddenly appeared before the hall. The King immediately descended from his seat and paid him great respect.
The King asked, "For what reason has the Master come? The śramaṇa replied, "This maidservant belongs to my patron's household."
"Maidservant, although you loathe my form, I shall not abandon you. May the King deign to show compassion and grant you your life.
The King said, "You must follow the Master’s command. At that time, I listened to his words and, with inner repentance, unexpectedly cried out:
"Namo to the Great Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha! Immediately following that cry, all the criminals in the hall who were within range of the sound had their shackles and manacles removed.
The shackles, stocks, and fetters were spontaneously released; his body did not appear. At that time, King Yama sat with eyes closed.
A śramaṇa took his hand and led him out of the hall. Immediately, he regained consciousness. His patron, Lady Li, hearing these words, revered the image all the more.
Throughout the entire prefecture, there was none who did not believe in his spiritual response.
Fourth: The Record of the Golden-Clad Kṣitigarbha Saving His Parents at the House of the Zu Family in Fuzhou during the Tang Dynasty.
The Prefectural Governor of Fuzhou, a member of the Zu family, possessed a sincere and firm faith; however, his parents had little belief from their youth. For his father’s sake, Zu...

The mother gave away her money and silks to have a single golden image of Kṣitigarbha made, three feet in height, a standing figure with a halo, to which she offered worship and contemplation with utmost devotion.
Her father was a native of Yangdu; having gone abroad on some business, the mother lived alone.

An evil thief secretly watched for an opportunity to steal her clothing, but saw only the seated Kṣitigarbha. The next day, changing his clothes, he went to her house and saw the patriarch [the image].

The mother-in-law resided there, having adorned her body with ornaments, yet she did not see the sacred image. The thief found this strange and personally confessed his gratitude, recounting what he had seen during the night;
he did not know of her spiritual power. When the father returned home, the mother told him of these previous events, and they were able to verify the account together.
Later, his father traveled to Fuzhou. On the road, he encountered an enemy; he immediately drew a sharp blade and struck him down.

There was a śramaṇa whose body was golden in color, who parried the blade with his hand and received the blow upon his head. Though he suffered injury and lay on the ground, the enemy thought he had already been killed and dispersed.
The father, marvelling at this miraculous escape from harm, went to the house of the Zu family and related the preceding events in detail.
Filled with a sense of rare wonder, they went together to the place where the image was to pay their respects. Upon seeing the image, they noticed three sword-marks upon its head;

the golden hue had slightly faded, appearing as if blood were still flowing from them. Realizing that Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva had taken the blades upon himself to rescue his parents from peril, the father developed faith and the grandfather went to welcome the mother.
The three of them resided in Fuzhou, where they paid homage and made offerings day and night. [The father reached] seventy years of age.
When Jiufang passed away, thirty-five days elapsed. Daokuang then dreamed that his father’s body was suffused with radiance;

he moved freely through the air, flying back and forth. Struck by this rare wonder, Daokuang prostrated himself from afar toward his father and inquired after him, asking, "In what place have you been reborn?"
He replied, "I was born in the fourth heaven. Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha guided me to serve the one who is next to attain Buddhahood (the Upapadya).

Those born in that heaven are mostly guided by Great Beings (Mahāsattvas). Regarding the praise for the Upapadya, it says: 'The Great Being must not disregard the command of the Buddhas. It also says:
'Thirteen years from now, your life will end and you shall be reborn; your current body, however, will only be reborn after twenty-five years.'"
"Your wife shall give birth only after twenty-eight years. Having spoken these words, he vanished and did not appear again.

Subsequently, both the mother and her husband, the grandfather, experienced exactly what their father had foretold. One should know that when a single person creates an image, both parent and child will receive manifest benefits.
From that time onward, throughout the entire province, those who create images—whether sculpted or painted—and pay them homage and offerings have come to understand this.
Lin: Many instances of manifest responses.
*Record of Miraculous Responses by Sengjun of the Capital*, Volume Five.
Sengjun of the capital was surnamed Wang. After he entered the monastic order, he managed monastic affairs and committed numerous acts of misappropriation. Not...
He observed the precepts, yet his three karmas were unrestrained; he had never cultivated roots of goodness.
Since he lacked both virtuous conduct and the cultivation of merit, he died from a minor illness. His left and right flanks remained slightly warm, and after three days had passed, he revived.
Weeping, he threw himself upon the ground and recounted the events of the nether realm, saying: "When I was about to die, two officials of the underworld drove me away..."
He pursued [the monk] to the front of the Great City Gate. Suddenly, a monk appeared and said, "I am Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.

When you were in the capital, you fashioned a statue of me; yet, without offering worship or making offerings, you cast it away behind a great temple. I must now requite you for this act of molding my image.
Since you are a master of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, I shall teach you a single line of text, which says: 'If a person wishes to fully comprehend...'"
"Know this: one should contemplate all Buddhas of the three periods of time in this way—the mind creates all Tathāgatas.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha to him. "If one can recite this verse, it can close the gates of hell, open the path to the Pure Land, and enable one to announce their name to King Yama.
Once the monk Jun had mastered the recitation of this verse, he entered the city.
He saw King Yama. The King then asked, "Since you were born during the time of the Dharma, what merit do you possess?

He replied, "I was foolish and negligent, unable to cultivate goodness. I served the affairs of the monastery and could not maintain the precepts; I did nothing but receive and uphold this single practice, this four-line verse."

The King asked, "Do you still recite it? He replied, "I remember what I have recited," and he recited the aforementioned verse in its entirety. At that moment, all those suffering from the sound of his voice attained liberation.
The King said, "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak further. Release him and let him return to the human world. Due to these circumstances, Su was revived.
Furthermore, he spoke to the Huayan Dharma Master, a śramaṇa learned in the treatises, to re-examine the text of the verse; thus he came to know that it was [the work of]...

In the twelfth chapter of the *Avataṃsaka*, titled "The Chapter on the Assembly of Immeasurable Bodhisattvas in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven," there is the prose by the Bodhisattva Tathāgatarāja praising the Buddha.
This text was frequently expounded to the monks of various temples by Sengjun;
those who heard it were moved to resolve their minds [to seek awakening], and they simply came to believe and accept the *Avataṃsaka*.
The *Huayan zhuan* (Biographies of the Avataṃsaka) has lost its author’s name. It was recounted by Wang Shi himself to the monk Dingfa of Kongguan Temple.
Now, I have examined its beginning and end.
This is the sixth fascicle of the *Dizang ganying ji* (Records of the Responsive Manifestations of Kṣitigarbha), transcribed by the monk Dingfa of Kongguan Temple.
Śramaṇa Dingfa of Kongguan Temple, together with Śramaṇa Jun, copied the accounts of Kṣitigarbha’s miraculous responses. They placed their particular reliance and faith upon this Bodhisattva;
every month on the fast days, they would copy [the images], prostrate, and make offerings.

After three years had passed, while he was praying for a manifestation of the Bodhisattva to appear in response to a desperate matter, a young śramaṇa came to stay overnight in the corridor of the temple.
Dingfa heard these words and respectfully came out to greet him. After exchanging a few words, the visitor suddenly vanished.
People marveled at this and asked Dingfa, "What did that visiting śramaṇa say? Dingfa replied, "The śramaṇa said, 'Your vow is already fulfilled; why is your spirit so low-spirited? and so forth.
Those who heard this all said, "You worry about seeing Kṣitigarbha, yet you do not contemplate the essential means of liberation. Therefore, [the Bodhisattva...]"
The Bodhisattva manifested his body and said, "Why is your resolve so short? You must certainly manifest [the truth] and give rise to the bodhicitta, joyfully seeking the unsurpassed path.
As a result, he appeared in a dream and said: "The śramaṇa who was here previously is Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
Because you sought to see my body without giving rise to the bodhicitta, I have awakened you. You have made many copies of my form, yet you will never..."

Having fallen into the three evil realms, he abandoned his life and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. On the day the Compassionate Honored One descended to be born, he was destined to receive the Buddha’s prophecy.
I followed you in accordance with your will, like a shadow following a form, or water conforming to its vessel. Moved by awakening, my tears fell like rain;

I immediately relinquished my robes, bowl, and possessions to create a statue equal in size to your body. Within the carved body of the statue, I collected images that had been drafted over many years, to which I paid homage and made offerings.
It was as if radiant light were emitted; how manifest was its spiritual efficacy!
This is the seventh record of the layman Li Xinsi, who was spared from the calamity of ghosts by Kṣitigarbha.
The layman Li Xinsi was a native of Lushui. The men and women of his household were being tormented by malevolent spirits.
More than thirty people lay unconscious in pain; some vomited crimson blood, while others fell into deep stupor.
At that time, Xinsi was filled with grief and distress, and he questioned the monks regarding the methods for rescue and deliverance. After reflecting for a long while, the śramaṇa told him:
"In the past, when the Tathāgata was in the world, at the gate of the house of the elder Kautika beneath Mount Vipula in the kingdom of Magadha, [he was struck on] the head..."
An evil spirit had stolen their vital essence, and five hundred members of the household all lay in a state of stupor and unconsciousness for ten days.
At that time, Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, while traveling and teaching throughout various lands, arrived at the elder’s house and gave rise to a heart of great compassion.
He recited mantras to save them, and all were healed at once. You should follow his method and take refuge in the Honored One Kṣitigarbha;
then you will always experience joy. Jianmeiquan lost the original painting of his image, yet within fifty years, Lushui County was spared from the fear of disease.
That miraculous image remains to this day.
The Eighth Record of Miraculous Responses of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva Saving Sentient Beings in Hell at Kaishan Temple.
At Mount Zhong’s Kaishan Temple, there is a statue of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, three feet in height, with the surrounding halo measuring four feet five inches in total.
For many years, it was unknown who had created [this image]. Later, when Director of the Yang Commandery Deng Zong was sixty-one years old, he fell slightly ill and was about to die;
his heart remained warm. Before the funeral rites were performed, he revived after one day and one night.
Weeping bitterly and unable to speak, he was supported by his descendants as he went before Kaishan Temple and said to the monks, "The Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha is here within this [image]."

The image was three feet high, with its halo measuring four feet five inches; it was somewhat damaged. [Deng Zong] did not wish to prostrate or make offerings to it, and the monks did not know where it was located.

Following Deng Zong’s words, he searched among the various sacred images. Having identified what was called the "Image According to Words," he prostrated his head in reverence and informed the monks of his desire to invite this image.
The monks asked about his intentions, and he replied: "When I die, I suddenly see the Four Grades."

The official was driven to the great city gate and stood there bewildered for a moment. The official entered the city and, after a short while, came out and said to me, "You may attend before the hall.
I immediately went before the King. The King said, "You must not die; furthermore, you uphold the Dharma as your family vocation.
You shall soon return to the human realm. However, the path of the netherworld is terrifying, and people do not realize this. You—"

"Do you wish to see hell? He replied, "I wish to see it. The Master immediately summoned an official in green robes and said, "Take Deng Zong to hell and show him the various instruments of suffering.
They then departed the city with the official and traveled northeast for a distance of about five or six li.
There was a great iron city with gates made of iron that opened and closed. As he drew near, he saw it; within the city, fierce fires blazed intensely, with sparks flying like those from a forge.
Hundreds of thousands of sinners were suffering there. At that time, a certain śramaṇa entered the prison to ward off the fierce flames and instructed the sinners;
consequently, the flames momentarily subsided. He then advanced further to the iron city, where there were eighteen hells.
Within it, the manner of their suffering cannot be fully described. While there, the śramaṇa instructed the sinners as before;
after inspecting each one in turn, he returned. Emerging from hell, the śramaṇa spoke, saying, "Do you know me?
They replied, "We do not know you. After a long while, he said, "I am Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva of Kaishan Temple."
In the past, the Dharma Master Zhiman, a disciple of the Śramaṇa Dharma Master Zhizang, carved an image of me in order to save sentient beings suffering in the three miserable realms.
I granted his prayer and, at one specific time each day, entered the eighteen great hells and the immeasurable minor hells to instruct and guide them.
Those with strong seeds from previous lives would resolve their minds and ascend out; those with weaker seeds would plant the seeds for future emergence.

As for those with evil causes who are most base and feeble—even down to those who have severed their roots of goodness, hold wrong views, and lack any virtue—they neither perceive nor know, and they possess no intention at all to escape.
If such persons are among humans, those whose roots of goodness are weak are easy to approach, convert, and deliver.

However, if people enter the evil realms, the power of the sages is ineffective, for they are like wood or stone. As for these who do not perceive, one must wait until the time of their future emergence. If...

Regarding those who are slightly strong: at the very beginning of their entry, they may give rise to a mind of repentance, thinking, "By the power of the Dharma you have upheld, I shall escape the sufferings of hell and return early to the human realm;
I ought to report this matter. They then raise their eyes to gaze up at the śramaṇa, whose body is three feet tall and permeated by light that destroys [all defilements].
Furthermore, he bestows two verses, saying: "If one is in the human realm, one can cultivate the Way; even for an icchantika, if they possess the heart [to seek it], it is still possible."
[The Buddha] set out. If the karma for entering an evil realm has already ripened, the mind is devoid of discernment and cannot be saved.
It is like an elderly person wishing to travel on a road: if they move their feet, they can proceed with assistance; but if they lie down, their strength is insufficient to move.

The fixed karma of sentient beings is likewise. Having spoken these verses, he suddenly vanished. Whether awake or asleep, he kept this matter in mind, fearing that if it were not true, he might speak of it to others in vain.
A person saw this image today; it was exactly as he had previously seen it. For this reason, he wished to invite it away. When the monks heard this, they said with joy, "Excellent!
Your faith has moved the holy one to manifest his record. You may only copy and restore it, but you must not invite it away.
Thereupon, they hired a skilled artisan to make a copy while leaving the original intact. Thus, both the new and old images remain together for all to behold with a devoted heart.
The Ninth Record of the Response of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva by a Widow of Mengzhou.

Regarding the widow of Mengzhou (whose name has been lost): tradition holds that this woman daily served the Dharma with diligence, remained chaste and forever renounced marriage, and lived a life of lifelong solitude.
She resolved to paint an image of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, but lacked the necessary funds; she therefore sought them from her relatives and friends.
He paid nineteen copper coins to hire an artisan to paint it. The image was eight inches in height, including the halo, and was merely a sketch in ink; the colors had not yet been applied.
At that time, the country was beset by turmoil, and the image was lost. It was only after more than a year of peace that he sought the image to add the colors, but he did not know where it was.
He lamented and meditated upon it day and night, until suddenly he was afflicted by demonic interference for over a month, which caused his nights to turn into days.
Recalling the image from the past, she contemplated seeking its protection. In a dream, she saw the image upon her pillow; it extended its right hand and stroked her body.
Upon awakening, she said to herself, "The image is clearly here on my pillow. Although the silk was slightly damaged, the painted figure itself showed no decay at all.
Overjoyed, she enshrined it within her room, where she paid homage and made offerings. At that time, a close friend advised the widow, saying, "My daughter..."
The body has three stages of dependence: in youth, one depends on one's parents; in middle age, one depends on one's husband; in old age, one depends on one's children.
Since you have lost your parents and have neither a husband nor children, when you reach old age, who will support and care for you? You must follow my instructions.
Seeking a husband for her daughter, the woman said: "Couples who stand side by side but have no offspring fill our ears and eyes;
even those with children do not necessarily raise them. In truth, this is a minor matter. It is the same as preparing for the karma of birth and death. She declined and did not follow her words.

She simply prayed to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, vowing that she would not die prematurely in her decline and ignorance. One night, she was moved by a dream in which a śramaṇa appeared holding a precious jewel;

Upon waking, the hair on her body stood on end, and she abandoned the intent to take her own life. Those who heard of it marveled at it. When the months were complete, she gave birth to a son and a daughter.
Their forms and features were dignified and beautiful. The girl remembered her previous dream and named the boy Jizang (Earth Store); the girl was named... [name omitted].
They were named Ruyi (Wish-Fulfilling). The two sons possessed filial piety from their youth, such that those who saw them felt moved with compassion.
They provided them with clothing and food and drink, so that mother and sons together had no anxiety over their sustenance. Everyone said they were the response of a sage.

At one time, the two sons were gone together and no one knew where they had gone; they did not return for three days. When the mother asked the reason for this, the elder son replied, "I went to the West, to the Land of Peace."
"It is a land of bliss. One beholds the assembly of bodhisattvas and holy ones there; Mother, you should aspire to be born in that land," and so forth.
The daughter said, "I shall go to the Tuṣita Heaven to pay homage to Maitreya. Men and women fill its midst; Mother, will you also aspire to be born there? The mother replied:
"I am weary of this female body and do not delight in celestial pleasures. Even if I were born in the heavens, I fear I would still receive a female body.
Now I must vow for the Pure Land of the West. Her two sons were filled with joy. The mother repaired an ancient earthen image of the Buddha and practiced mindfulness of the Buddha.
At the age of seventy-eight, she passed away. Two streams of white light descended from the sky and covered her body; she rose into the air for a brief moment and pointed toward the west.
Just as they were dispersing, the two sons abandoned their house to establish a vihāra, naming it Ruyi Temple (Yìrúì Sì).

The brothers both left the household life together and exhorted others to take refuge in Dizang, saying that those who witnessed his miraculous responses were numerous. Later, they lost track of where he had gone; how much more so for those who do not know the beginning or the end.
The temple still exists today, though it has fallen into considerable ruin.
The Tenth Record of the Miraculous Response of Kṣitigarbha Carved on the Head of a Staff from the Household of Minister Deng of Jianzhou in the Tang Dynasty.
Minister Deng of the Deng clan in Jinshui County, Jianzhou, saw by the side of a road near his neighbor’s house a broken staff-head carved with the image of a monk.
Not recognizing it as a statue, the Secretariat Drafter—who was a devout believer in Buddhism—carried it home, inserted it into his wall, paid his respects, and departed.
He did not destroy it again. After two or three years had passed, he suddenly fell ill and died; his chest remained slightly warm, so they hesitated to bury him.
Only after a day and a night did he revive. Rising up, he wept and recounted the circumstances of his journey through the netherworld, saying: "At the moment of my death..."
Two riders came from the path of the dead, galloping and rushing until they reached the gate of the great city.
They dismounted from their horses and led me into the city, arriving before the king’s hall. There I saw hundreds of thousands of people in the courtyard, bound in shackles and fetters.
The king was filled with rage and intended to rebuke me. At that moment, a śramaṇa appeared, his appearance hideous and his head shaped like a goblin’s; he stepped forward.
Upon arriving before the hall, the king saw him from afar and paid him respectful homage. Rising from his seat, he joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and said:
"O Great Sage, Śramaṇa, for what reason have you come here so suddenly? [The Buddha] replied: "You should say to the Minister of State: 'He is a donor (dānapati).'"
"I wish to repay his kindness; you may be spared and saved. The King replied, "Since my karma is already fixed, both my life and my provisions for food are exhausted;

such a thing is difficult to achieve. The Śramaṇa said, "In the past, within the Sudharmā Hall of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, I received the Buddha’s entrustment that I am able to save even sentient beings whose karma is fixed.
This is not the case for the first time today; how much more so for a Minister who has not committed a grave offense?"
“Is this not a sin? Why do you not rescue me? The King said, “A Great Being’s great vows are as firm and immovable as a mountain of diamond.
You must be released and returned to the human world. Once his food was exhausted, the King granted him some small beans. The śramaṇa rejoiced and led the youth by the hand toward the path of life;
having bid each other farewell, they departed. The youth entreated the śramaṇa, saying, “Wait but a moment; who is it that will save me? No.

The official examined him and said, "Do you not know me? I am Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. In the past, when you were among humans, you saw my image by the side of a road, yet you did not recognize it at all.
You placed it within a wall; while playing as a child, you fashioned a staff with a head carved like an image, but it had only a head and no other features.
For this reason, its form was ugly. Can you remember this? Having spoken these words, he continued:
Suddenly, it vanished. This was a supreme manifestation. When both monastics and laypeople heard of it, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

Inside the wall of the Master’s residence, within a corner of the stable, they saw an image on the tip of a staff. Having divided the staff and refashioned it with carvings and engravings, using sandalwood as a companion material, they produced a five-inch image.
The image emitted a brilliant light that illuminated the interior of the house. Thereupon, the Master had a life-sized image fashioned.

Within it, he enshrined a small image and established a temple for those who had left the household life, naming it Jizō-dai (Kṣitigarbha Terrace). People from near and far gazed upon it as if looking at a marketplace;
such was the extent of Kṣitigarbha’s transformative guidance and beneficial influence. This was the very pinnacle of his deeds.
Record of the Miraculous Response Received by Śramaṇa Fashang of Huiri Monastery in Hua Prefecture, Tang Dynasty, Number Eleven.
Śramaṇa Fashang of Huiri Monastery was thirty-seven years of age when he left the household life; his family had made the practice of the Dharma their vocation. While residing at...
In the past, my family was engaged in hunting. While roaming through the forests and wilds, they repeatedly saw light emanating from within a thicket.

Suspecting it to be extraordinary, they sent a mounted attendant to investigate, who found nothing there but a piece of decayed wood about a foot long. He brought it back home. The next day, they saw the same light emanating from that same thicket as before.
They used a bamboo flute to probe the thicket and cleared away the decaying heartwood bit by bit, finding absolutely nothing remaining. They marveled at this and returned. Later—

While out on a hunting expedition, he saw that the light emanating from the previous thicket was no different than before. A sense of wonder arose in his mind, and he took the heartwood of a decayed tree, placed it upon a stump, and returned.

On the way back, he encountered a pack of tigers. He galloped his horse in pursuit of them; he drew his bow to shoot, but the string snapped. He searched through his quiver for a replacement string, but there was none.
As the fierce tigers turned back toward him, he fled in terror. His horse stumbled and fell, and he thought to himself that he had been mangled by the beasts.
He lost consciousness as if in a dream. He saw what appeared to be a śramaṇa pursuing him like a fierce tiger and asked, "Who are you?
The figure replied, "I am Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. [The man] said, "In a thicket, I saw a piece of rotten wood; that was my own body.
My great-great-grandfather established a temple on this site and fashioned my image. The temple has since fallen into ruin, and my image has decayed until only the heartwood remains."

"Because you were a descendant of Sun Xingyin, you beheld my radiance; therefore, I now rescue you," and so forth. Ryōkaku saw the horse neighing beside him as it stood still, while the fierce tiger did not know where to go.

He repented and reproached himself. In front of the shrine hall that had been established by the light he had previously seen, he fashioned an image of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva using weathered wood and clay.
He devotedly upheld the Dharma and once again continued the lamp of the teachings at Etsunichi-ji.
He abandoned this. The Dharma Catalogue lists seventy-eight [entries]. On the twenty-fourth day of the second month of that year, he told his companions:
"The Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha came to my house and said, 'Among the three assemblies where Maitreya Tathāgata expounds the Dharma, you were one who attained the Way during the second assembly.
Today you have relinquished your life-span and will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. I addressed the Great Being, saying, 'Heaven..."
The above are the realms of the five desires, whose pleasures are beyond compare. They cause one to lose sight of the bodhicitta.

Furthermore, if one hopes for a future Buddha, that time will still be long. Therefore, I only wish to be reborn in the Western World of Peace and Bliss. The Bodhisattva said: "This too shall be according to your vow.
If you wish to be born in the Pure Land, you should contemplate Amitābha Buddha with single-minded devotion for one day and one night."
The Buddha immediately attained rebirth. Having heard this supreme instruction, from yesterday onward he had focused his mind exclusively on the Buddha of the Western Quarter;
at that very moment, he was reborn in the Pure Land. Having said this, he joined his palms toward the direction of the West.

Those who witnessed it all said, "This is the rare and auspicious omen of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva emitting light and returning to the Pure Land. However, those who saw it were only two or three out of ten people.
Record of the Miraculous Response of Chen Du’s Daughter, Who Created an Image of Kṣitigarbha to Save Her Mother, Number Twelve.
Tradition says: Chen Du, the Regional Commander, had a young daughter surnamed Chen (her personal name is lost). She lost her mother while still young; day and night...
Longing for her yet not having seen her, the Prefect first enticed her, saying, "I am also your relative. Although your mother has passed away, your father still lives.

Why do you not communicate with him regarding food and drink, wishing instead to die? If you truly yearn for your deceased mother, you must create an image of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva and vow to pray for deliverance from suffering.
She then gave up five hundred coins to hire craftsmen to carve a three-foot statue, which she then brought back to her father’s home.
In the middle [of the night], she said to her father, "Please place my mother’s bed here. If you wish to see your mother, you shall see her in this image.

The father was moved by compassion; he vacated his own chamber and placed the sacred image there. The daughter worshipped and made offerings day and night, praying that her mother might be saved from suffering.
She dreamed of a śramaṇa who told the Lady Chen, "Your mother is in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell. I am..."

thereupon, he resolved upon *bodhicitta* to assist sentient beings. Moved by your supreme filial piety, my body entered hell to emit light and preach the Dharma, whereby your mother was freed from suffering and reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
As for the girl of the Chen family, she saw the robes of a śramaṇa scorched.
Sun asked him about the circumstances. The śramaṇa said, "When entering hell, it was merely like this blazing fierce fire. Upon waking, he was filled with both grief and joy.
When the assembled crowd saw the image, its clothes had changed color, appearing as if scorched by fire. Everyone in the household considered this a rare occurrence;
many who heard of it made copies of the image to represent their parents seeking rescue from suffering.
The Thirteenth Record of Lady Zhang of Yangzhou, Who Modeled Her Life on the Mother of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva to Deliver Beings from Suffering:
Lady Zhang was the legitimate daughter of Zhang Jianxin, the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Yangzhou. After her mother passed away, she was visited in a dream.

"Zhangshi, I raised you. Yet you indulged in greed and desire, and your arrogance was always extreme; because of this, you have received this retribution as a hungry ghost, suffering that is unbearable.
Take her with you. The daughter then asked about the nature of the suffering, and her mother said, "I am a ghost-child."
Day and night there is birth and death. Why is this? Those with heavy retribution as hungry ghosts eat their own children;
they eat them as soon as they are born, being unaware of death or birth. When they see their own biological mother, it is as if they see a great malevolent spirit.
However, for one day within a human month, they cannot eat me—specifically on the morning of the twenty-fourth day of the month. At that time, a monk entered the city.
Having been satiated with food through this offering, on all other days they cannot escape this suffering. At that time, the śramaṇa uttered these words: "I am the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha;
I have now entered the city of hungry ghosts to bestow great peace and happiness. You should all resolve to attain bodhicitta.
(Text) Although they heard these words, because they were bound by the retribution of their karma, they were unable to resolve their minds toward awakening; it lasted for only a single day.
"There is no end to their hunger and thirst" (and so forth). "If you wish to rescue them from this suffering, you must create an image of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
After her mother had instructed her in these matters, she awoke from her dream. Lady Zhang then exhausted her mother’s estate to create a life-sized image of Kṣitigarbha.
Later, he dreamed of his mother. Her body emitted a brilliant light as she stood in the midst of space and said to him:

Both took the same opportunity to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma. After waking, they were moved by profound sorrow. Those who heard of this came to make offerings to the image, and each received benefit.
This concludes the fourteenth record of the miraculous responses of Kṣitigarbha, compiled by Ju Tong, Prefect of Luzhou.
The entrustment concerning the matter of finding a path amidst the snow;

the entrustment concerning the matter of escaping demonic calamities to Kang Jutong, the Regional Inspector of Lu Province. His faith had long been sincere and virtuous, and for many years he had served the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha.
He further resolved to paint an image of the Honored One; before the various colors were even finished, a brilliant light shone forth. Tong’s faith grew even more profound.
He also dreamed that two mounted officers of the imperial guard were pursuing him; at that time, Tong could not escape and stood there in terror.
The officers dismounted and asked Tong, saying, "We have made a mistake regarding you. You are the donor for the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha. Our King..."

The lay devotee of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva had committed grave transgressions, yet [the Bodhisattva] did not allow him to fall into ruin. After the [devotee] spoke, he fell into a deep sleep; upon awakening, his faith and veneration became even more profound, and he made extensive offerings.
In the first year of the Guangming era of Emperor Xizong, malevolent spirits rose up in chaos, and those who died of disease in the realm became mountains.
He had a vision in which hundreds of thousands of blue ghosts passed by his gate, saying, "This house is the chamber of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva;
we are his subordinates and must not enter. Upon waking, he was filled with great joy, and he ensured that all the men and women of his household were spared from the calamity of these ghosts.
During the Zhonghe era, while traveling to the distant frontier on business, he encountered heavy snow on the road and lost his way; he then called upon Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
Sa. Once he saw a parrot hopping upon the snow; finding this strange, he pursued it. Before long, he found the correct path.
This was the "Contemplation of the Bodhisattva’s Responsive Manifestation. During the Guangqi era, Tong (87) suffered from a slight illness.

He prayed with such sincerity that he was cured. He had a dream in which a young monk said to him: "Because you killed a green sparrow, you fell into hell. Now I am making you repay that karma. It was only...
After enduring this for about one or two days, he was born in the Pure Land on the following day. "Do not harbor resentment toward me.
When his dream ended and he awoke, he prostrated with joy. On that very day, his illness was completely cured, and he passed away with right mindfulness. And so forth.
The Fifteenth Record of Miraculous Manifestations: The Three-Inch Sandalwood Image of Kṣitigarbha Made by Jianke, the Vice-Governor of Yongzhou.
Regarding Jianke, the Vice-Governor:
his faith was pure and clear, and he took the service of the Dharma as his primary purpose. One day, while fasting internally, he questioned a monk about [the practice of] laypeople.
"Householder, which Buddha or Bodhisattva do you intend to serve? You wish for benefit in both worlds. Regarding this, the various monks have differing opinions. Some say:
'Worship Avalokiteśvara, for he is the one who bestows fearlessness upon this Sahā world. Others say: 'Worship the Buddha Bhaiṣajyaguru, for there is a vow for benefit during the Semblance Dharma.
Others say: 'Worship Maitreya, for he is the future Guide. Others say: 'Worship Kṣitigarbha, for he has received the Buddha’s command. Thus, you may serve [whichever you choose]."
“Ksitigarbha, my heart’s desire is to show you this. Since it is the Buddha’s command, how could I abandon you?
She immediately sought sandalwood to fashion a three-inch image, which she placed within her hair-knot. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, she recited his name.

During the Chengtian era of Emperor Zhuangzong, when matters became desperate and the world was in turmoil due to war, Jianke was surrounded by rebel troops; he did not know where to flee and faced certain death.
In an instant, while he was holding the image in a single thought, a great general riding by saw him and, struck with alarm as their blades met, cried out to his companion:

"The one we were seeking is none other than Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva! How could we have mistakenly harmed a holy being? They immediately abandoned their pursuit, and the soldier found it a rare and wondrous occurrence.
After the turmoil of war had subsided, he recounted these circumstances to various monks, and those who heard it marveled at its strangeness.

During the Changxing era, while he was traveling to his official post, an enemy who had heard of this intended to inflict harm upon him; he waited for him at a key location on the road. The enemy saw only a śramaṇa passing by and did not see the monk at all.
Later, when he heard that [the monk] had already passed through, he repented and apologized, resolving his enmity. Furthermore, during the night on the road...
While staying overnight, it rained heavily, and the lamps were all extinguished. The image within [his] topknot emitted light that illuminated the lodging like the sun.
Suddenly, a voice like that of a young child said, "Depart quickly! Depart quickly! Startled and filled with wonder, he took the light as his guide and departed from the lodging.

The next day, a great flood surged up. His dwelling was at the bottom of this water, and he did not know how deep the abyss was. He thought to himself, "I am being protected by Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
He died at the age of seventy-eight; this was in the second year of the Qingtai era. At the time of his passing:
An image within his topknot emitted radiance; he bowed to the Buddha, joined his palms, and awaited death. That radiance rose toward the heavens for a brief moment.
Everyone said, "The light is escorting Jianke; he will certainly be reborn in heaven."
Record of the Miraculous Response of Kṣitigarbha, Part Sixteen: The Account of Cui Li-xi.
Cui Li-xi was the Governor of Chang’an and the younger brother of Minister Cui Long. In the second year of the Kaifu era, he died of thirst.
After two days, he revived and recounted his experiences in the realm of the dead, saying: "When I first died, two officials supported me under my armpits and led me away.
I also saw soldiers on white horses driving me forward. I do not know how many *li* we traveled, but I knew we had arrived at a great city in the northeast.
Facing the black gate, I entered from the south and saw the eastern gate; facing the black gate, I entered from the west and saw the southern gate."
Entering north through the Black Gate, one sees more than ten tiled-roofed buildings, each consisting of over ten bays.

Within them are thousands of rafters and various official hats and crowns, all of which are black in color. On both sides of these tiled-roofed buildings stand more than thirty stone records, all of which state:
"I am the Prefect. Furthermore, fifty-odd paces to the southwest, there are five stone records.
After about ten days, Li Xi approached the Prefect. The Prefect asked, "Whom do you serve?
Xi replied, "I serve the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha and provide offerings to various śramaṇas. The Prefect said again, "Since you serve a Great Sage, this is indeed a heavenly blessing.
The people then asked the minor official, "Has this man's life come to an end? The Prefect immediately—
He took up a scroll of writing with small characters and read it himself. He told Xiē, saying, "Your life has not yet reached its end; Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva has protected you.
He then called to the minor clerk, saying, "Why did you seize the life of one who belongs to the Buddha's family?
He then punished the clerk Bái Mǎ by tying him to a pillar for one day. He asked again, "Do you wish to return alone? He replied, "I wish to return. [The official] sent him back to the prefecture.
The Lord said, "You wish to see hell? He replied, "I wish to see it. The Lord of the Prefecture pointed toward a horse and three scribes, and they departed from the northeast.
After traveling some five or six *li*, they saw a great iron city several tens of *li* square.
Within it was an iron house filled with boiling iron and blazing fires. Next, they inspected a tiled-roofed house.

The gates were made of iron. The official of the underworld opened the iron gates and allowed him to see them. As he looked closely, he saw his grandfather, great-grandfather, and others, all within that city.
Their bodies were bound with cangues, shackles, and manacles, and they were encircled by fierce fires that were scorching their limbs to a pulp.
Seeing them thus bound, he wept and said, "You must save me! They replied, "We shall..."
He called upon the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha. As he proceeded forward, he saw a city. Within it was a bed of glowing iron upon which one lay.
It was the śramaṇa he had previously seen, sitting there with his body like charcoal, amidst a fierce fire blazing intensely. He asked, "Master, you practiced the holy life."
"Why is it so now? The śramaṇas replied, "We practiced the holy life for the sake of fame and gain;

because our inner thoughts and outward conduct were no longer in accord, the bedding, seats, and other items we previously used have turned into instruments of great suffering, and our robes, food, and drink have turned into iron garments and molten copper. Donor, you must save us! He said:
"Master, you should call to mind Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. You saw some dozens of hells, each filled with agonizing torments and replete with sinners;
these were all people you had seen among the living. Furthermore, as you advanced, you saw red sand, trees with sword-like blades, and pillars of molten copper.
Hundreds of thousands of sinners were there, prostrating themselves against the pillars, all shedding tears as they were bound. You should..."

"Save us! they cried. [The guide] said, "You must constantly keep the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha in mind. Thus, the seven hells of yellow sand, white sand, parched sand, and so forth, were all seen as described above.
Thereupon, he returned. He next saw houses made of green-tiled sand, with clear, soaring beams of precious materials measuring seven or eight inches.
To his left and right were jeweled trees, laden with various fruits. He then questioned the two attendants.

The official said, "Among the disciples of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva who serve as patrons (dānapati), those who reverently paint his image will mostly be reborn in the Pure Lands or in Tuṣita Heaven, each according to their respective vows.
Those who do not believe in the images but still serve him will mostly dwell here for a time before proceeding further.
Look ahead into the great city, where you see a great jeweled palace and hundreds of thousands of millions of men and women sporting and playing."
Within that place, he further saw his parents, relatives, and kin greeting him with joy.

The various men and women said, "Previously, while we were in hell, it was because you taught us to recite the name of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva that we abandoned our suffering and were born here in this great palace.

His parents, brothers, and six kinds of kin spoke to him with delight, saying, "It is by the grace of your kindness and the transformative power of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva that we have been liberated."
Suffering arises in that place. Again he asked, "What is this place? He replied, "It is named Puṇyaśālā (The House of Merit). There one lives long and is far removed from all sufferings.
Although born therein, one will inevitably encounter the three assemblies of Maitreya and reach the end of all suffering. He asked again, "Who established this?
He replied, "Long ago, when the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha was in the world, he received the entrustment of the Tathāgata and said to the Buddha: 'Four...'"

My disciples shall certainly not fall into the evil realms. Within the interval of five billion six hundred and seventy million years between the appearance of Śākyamuni Buddha and the appearance of Maitreya Buddha, those who wish to be reborn in a pure land or in the fourth heaven but possess little merit—
They all entered this House of Merit and did not return to the evil realms, merely awaiting a future Buddha.
Returning to the presence of the Prefect, he immediately dispatched the two men ahead to escort them back, where they were revived. Upon hearing this, many people subsequently painted images of him.
Seventeenth: A Record of the Response of the Image of Kṣitigarbha Created by Guo Xuan’an, the Imperial Protector of Yizhou, during the Great Han.
Guo Xuan’an, the Imperial Protector of Yizhou, harbored a mind of disbelief and was biasedly devoted to Laozi. In the third year of Qiandao...

In the middle of the fifth lunar month of that year, I fell ill with a chronic fever due to the intense heat. Although I underwent medical treatment with a hundred methods, I could not escape it for long.

My wife, who was a devoted follower of the Buddha, consulted the deity Kṣitigarbha and was told, "You should make a vow; if you can create [an image of] Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva within a single day, the illness will be remitted.
Suddenly, the situation became urgent and could no longer be delayed. As I lay prostrate upon my sickbed, I still did not believe it and said, "I must make a vow..."
Regarding his vow: if there were any signs of spiritual resonance, he would believe it. One day, he suddenly fell into a state of unconsciousness.
His wife immediately looked up to heaven and wailed, shedding ten thousand streams of tears and breaking her heart and liver as she prayed to the various heavens for his restoration to life.
Those nearby who did not believe increased their slander and false views; those with biased minds all claimed it was the fault of not having taken refuge in Kṣitigarbha. After three...
Awakening three times during the night, he threw himself upon the ground and sought a sharp blade to cut out his own tongue; those who saw him thought he was insane.
Only after his wife comforted him did he finally calm down. He said, "You are a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*);

you have been able to prolong my life, remove the suffering of hell, grant me celestial bliss, and show me the path to liberation. His wife asked, "Please tell me the beginning and end of this matter; how did you recover?"

The king then examined a scroll of scripture which said: "If a person is profoundly filial and creates images or paints murals, their lifespan shall be long and far-reaching."
"I grant you forty years of extended life. Of these, for twenty years you shall fulfill the utmost filial piety;

for the remaining twenty years, you shall receive the rewards of a filial son. At that time, a minister dressed in green came forth, presented the document, and said to the King: "The life of Jianzi is but ten years."
"To whom shall I offer filial devotion? The King replied, "The Dharma King’s words are never twofold; you must prolong your life," and so forth.

Upon hearing these words, I immediately regained consciousness. When I spoke of this to those who heard it, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, exclaiming, "Kien (Gñānajñāna) truly still lives!"

I have long taken refuge in Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. Whether seeking out his ancient traces or consulting contemporary accounts, I have recorded over one hundred instances of his spiritual responses (*saṃyǐng*).
Among these, I have selected more than thirty of the most eminent cases.
Fearing that they might suddenly be lost and their manifestations sink into oblivion, I have hastily produced this record, noting them with direct penmanship; it preserves only a general outline.
It is my hope that there may be superior verification hereafter, so that this work may serve as a support for my own practice.
As for the other matters not recorded here, who would know them? Let this be a vow to inspire future faith.
Record of the Miraculous Efficacy of the Image of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, Scroll One.
